title: Genetic Oscillator Stability Analysis
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter works through a single worked example from Michael Savageau's biochemical systems theory (BST): the synthetic *E. coli* circuit of Atkinson, Savageau, Myers and Ninfa (*Cell* **113**, 597–607, 2003), which wires a short positive-feedback loop and a longer negative-feedback loop onto the same promoter and, depending on how the loops are tuned, makes the circuit behave either as a toggle switch or as an oscillator. The lecture's own stated goal is to derive the stability diagram that separates those regimes (its Fig. 1B). It assumes you already have linear stability analysis for a fixed point — that $\dot x = F(x)$ is locally stable at $x^*$ when every eigenvalue of the Jacobian $DF(x^*)$ has negative real part — and Savageau's power-law (S-system) description of a regulated promoter from earlier in the course. ## A circuit with two feedback loops The paper builds a genetic network out of the two-component signalling system NRI/NRI~P and the *lac* repressor LacI. Transcription of the gene for NRI (drawn as mRNA $X_1$) is controlled by a promoter that both **NRI~P** and **LacI** act on directly: NRI~P (the phosphorylated, active form of NRI, $X_2$) activates its own promoter — a short, direct positive-feedback loop — while LacI ($X_4$) represses the same promoter through a longer path: NRI~P first activates transcription of the gene for LacI (mRNA $X_3$), which is translated into LacI, which then loops back to repress $X_1$. A further step (mRNA $X_5$, repressed by LacI) drives *lacZ* ($X_6$), whose product $\beta$-galactosidase is the experimental readout — it sits downstream of the loop and does not feed back into it. The paper built two versions of the negative-feedback arm's promoter (its Fig. 2A and 2B, driving *lacI* from *glnKp* and from *lacIp* respectively), which retune the strength of the long loop relative to the short one; the same core topology is reported to produce either switch-like or oscillatory reporter time courses (its Figs. 1C–F and 3B–E) depending on that tuning. The given lecture materials don't include the figure legends that say which construct produced which behaviour, so that pairing isn't asserted here — only that both behaviours came out of the same network drawn above. ## A transcription–translation module Before writing the full cascade, the outline sets up its basic building block: an mRNA translated into a protein that decays (or is diluted by growth) at rate $\beta$. Odd subscripts are mRNAs, even subscripts are the proteins they encode. Translation of $X_1$ into protein $X_2$ is modelled as $$\frac{dX_2}{dt} = k_p X_1 - \beta_2 X_2 \tag{VII.17}$$ with $k_p$ the translation rate constant and $\beta_2$ the protein's decay rate constant. Normalizing each variable by its steady-state value, $x_i = X_i/X_i^{ss}$, and using $X_2^{ss} = (k_p/\beta_2) X_1^{ss}$ (the steady state of VII.17 itself) turns this into a dimensionless relaxation equation: $$\frac{dx_2}{dt} = \beta_2(x_1 - x_2) \tag{VII.18}$$ which is worth checking once: substituting $X_2 = X_2^{ss}x_2$ and $X_1=X_1^{ss}x_1$ into VII.17 gives $X_2^{ss}\dot x_2 = k_p X_1^{ss} x_1 - \beta_2 X_2^{ss} x_2$; dividing by $X_2^{ss}$ and using $k_pX_1^{ss}/X_2^{ss}=\beta_2$ leaves exactly VII.18. Every even-indexed equation in the full model below has this same shape — it is nothing but "translate, then decay," rewritten in units where the steady state is $1$. ## The six-variable cascade and its regulation functions Chaining two copies of this module together, with the odd equations carrying whatever transcriptional regulation acts on that mRNA, gives the system for the whole circuit: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{dx_1}{dt} &= \beta_1(f_1 - x_1) \\ \frac{dx_2}{dt} &= \beta_2(x_1 - x_2) \\ \frac{dx_3}{dt} &= \beta_3(f_3 - x_3) \\ \frac{dx_4}{dt} &= \beta_4(x_3 - x_4) \\ \frac{dx_5}{dt} &= \beta_5(f_5 - x_5) \\ \frac{dx_6}{dt} &= \beta_6(x_5 - x_6) \end{aligned} \tag{VII.19}$$ Only $x_1,\dots,x_4$ matter for stability: the loop closes at $X_4$ (LacI), and $x_5, x_6$ are the downstream reporter arm from the last section — they respond to whatever $x_4$ does but never feed back into it, so they cannot change whether the fixed point of the first four variables is stable. $f_1$ and $f_3$ describe the promoter's response, and are **tri-phasic**: a basal floor $B$ when the regulatory input is small, a graded power-law response in between, and a saturating ceiling $M$ when the input is large — the standard S-system description of a regulated promoter, with a floor and ceiling because real promoters can't be repressed or activated without limit. $$f_1 = \begin{cases} B & : x_2^{g_{12}} x_4^{g_{14}} < B \\ x_2^{g_{12}} x_4^{g_{14}} & : B < x_2^{g_{12}} x_4^{g_{14}} < M \\ M & : x_2^{g_{12}} x_4^{g_{14}} > M \end{cases} \tag{VII.20a}$$ $$f_3 = \begin{cases} B & : x_2^{g_{32}} < B \\ x_2^{g_{32}} & : B < x_2^{g_{32}} < M \\ M & : x_2^{g_{32}} > M \end{cases} \tag{VII.20b}$$ The exponents are Savageau's **logarithmic gains**, $g_{ij} = \partial \ln f_i/\partial \ln x_j$ evaluated on the graded branch — which is exactly what a power law $x_j^{g_{ij}}$ gives by construction. Their signs are fixed by the loop diagram above: $g_{12}>0$ since NRI~P activates its own promoter, $g_{14}<0$ since LacI represses that same promoter, and $g_{32}>0$ since NRI~P activates the *lacI* mRNA. The lecture's materials describe $f_5$ only by analogy (repression of $X_5$'s promoter by $X_4$, so presumably a single-exponent tri-phasic function like $f_3$) and don't give its exact form — it isn't needed for stability regardless. ## Linearizing at the fixed point Because $x_i$ is normalized by *a* steady-state value $X_i^{ss}$, whenever the normalized system has exactly one fixed point, that point is automatically $x_1=x_2=x_3=x_4=1$ — not because of anything special about this circuit, but because $X_i^{ss}$ was chosen to be the value at that fixed point, so $x_i=X_i/X_i^{ss}=1$ there by definition. This is the "single fixed point" case the outline restricts to; it implicitly also assumes the fixed point sits on the graded, middle branch of $f_1$ and $f_3$ (otherwise the corresponding partial derivative below is zero and that piece of feedback is locally switched off). Differentiating VII.19's first four equations at $x_1=x_2=x_3=x_4=1$ gives the Jacobian. Row 1 (from $\dot x_1=\beta_1(f_1-x_1)$) needs $\partial f_1/\partial x_2 = g_{12}x_2^{g_{12}-1}x_4^{g_{14}}\to g_{12}$ and $\partial f_1/\partial x_4 = g_{14}x_2^{g_{12}}x_4^{g_{14}-1}\to g_{14}$ at the fixed point; row 2 (from $\dot x_2 = \beta_2(x_1-x_2)$) is linear already. This is as far as the lecture outline's own transcription of the matrix goes before its conversion cuts off mid-row: $$A = \begin{bmatrix} -\beta_1 & \beta_1 g_{12} & 0 & \beta_1 g_{14} \\ \beta_2 & -\beta_2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \beta_3 g_{32} & -\beta_3 & \; ? \end{bmatrix}$$ The missing entry and the whole fourth row follow the same pattern, direct from VII.19: $f_3$ does not depend on $x_4$, so the $(3,4)$ entry is $0$; and $\dot x_4=\beta_4(x_3-x_4)$ is linear, giving row 4 exactly as row 2 was for $x_1,x_2$. Completing it: $$A = \begin{bmatrix} -\beta_1 & \beta_1 g_{12} & 0 & \beta_1 g_{14} \\ \beta_2 & -\beta_2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \beta_3 g_{32} & -\beta_3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \beta_4 & -\beta_4 \end{bmatrix}$$ ## From the Jacobian to the stability diagram $A$ has a block structure worth noticing before expanding the determinant: rows 2 and 4 only tie $x_2$ to $x_1$ and $x_4$ to $x_3$, while the feedback loop $X_1\to X_2\to X_3\to X_4\to X_1$ enters through $g_{12}$ (the short loop, direct) and through $g_{14}$ and $g_{32}$ together (the two edges of the long loop). Expanding $\det(A-\lambda I)$ along the column for $x_4$ makes this explicit: $$\det(A-\lambda I) = (\beta_3+\lambda)(\beta_4+\lambda)\Big[(\beta_1+\lambda)(\beta_2+\lambda) - \beta_1\beta_2 g_{12}\Big] \;-\; \beta_1\beta_2\beta_3\beta_4\, g_{14}g_{32}.$$ The second term is exactly minus the product of the four Jacobian entries around the feedback cycle ($\beta_2$ from $X_1\!\to\!X_2$, $\beta_3g_{32}$ from $X_2\!\to\!X_3$, $\beta_4$ from $X_3\!\to\!X_4$, $\beta_1g_{14}$ from $X_4\!\to\!X_1$) — which is why the stability diagram's axis is the *product* $g_{14}g_{32}$ rather than the two gains separately: they are the two regulated edges of one loop, and a loop only ever contributes to the determinant as a whole. Multiplying out gives a quartic $\lambda^4+a_1\lambda^3+a_2\lambda^2+a_3\lambda+a_4=0$ with $$a_1=\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3+\beta_4, \qquad a_4=\beta_1\beta_2\beta_3\beta_4\big[(1-g_{12})-g_{14}g_{32}\big],$$ and $a_2,a_3$ similar combinations of the $\beta_i$ and $g_{12}$ that don't involve $g_{14}g_{32}$ at all (only $a_4$ picks up the loop term, since only the loop term in the determinant above involves it). The classical Routh–Hurwitz test for a quartic says all four eigenvalues have negative real part exactly when $a_1>0$, $a_3>0$, $a_4>0$, and a fourth combination usually called $c_1 = a_1a_2a_3-a_3^2-a_1^2a_4$ is also positive. $a_1>0$ holds automatically here, since it is a sum of decay rates — leaving three genuine boundaries, which is exactly what the lecture's stability diagram draws. The $a_4>0$ boundary is the cleanest: since $\beta_1\beta_2\beta_3\beta_4>0$ always, $$a_4>0 \iff g_{14}g_{32} < 1-g_{12},$$ a straight line of slope $-1$ through $(g_{12},g_{14}g_{32})=(0,1)$ — matching the diagram's boundary exactly. The $a_3>0$ boundary is not as universal: $a_3$ depends on the individual $\beta_i$, not just their sum, so its threshold on $g_{12}$ in general depends on the decay-rate values too. As an illustration only (not asserted as what the paper assumed), pairing the two mRNA decay rates and the two protein decay rates, $\beta_1=\beta_3$ and $\beta_2=\beta_4$, collapses $a_3>0$ to the clean threshold $g_{12}<2$ regardless of the actual rate values — which is the vertical line the diagram shows. The third condition, $c_1>0$, is the remaining curve; expanding it needs $a_2$ and $a_3$ in full, which the outline doesn't carry out (its own text points to the paper's Supplementary Information for this), so it is not reproduced here. Crossing each boundary has a distinct meaning. $a_4=\det(-A)$ up to sign, so $a_4=0$ is where a real eigenvalue passes through zero — the mechanism by which extra real fixed points are born, which is consistent with the "multistable" label above that boundary (a toggle switch needs more than one stable state). Crossing $c_1=0$ while $a_3,a_4$ stay positive is, by the general theory, where a complex-conjugate pair of eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis: a damped spiral becomes a growing one, and because $f_1,f_3$ are bounded between $B$ and $M$ rather than truly linear, that local growth cannot diverge — it settles into a sustained limit cycle, matching "unstable (sustained oscillations)". The lecture's simulated reporter traces (its Fig. 1C–F) illustrate exactly this range: monostable switching between a high and a low steady state in one parameter setting, versus decaying oscillations in another, versus sustained periodic ones in a third; and its Fig. 3B–E overlay real $\beta$-galactosidase and glutamine synthetase measurements on the corresponding model fits, showing the same damped-oscillation behaviour experimentally. ## Sources - `lecture-outlines/11-outline.md` (this course, 2004, lecture 11) — the citation to Atkinson, Savageau, Myers & Ninfa, *Cell* **113**, 597–607 (2003); equations VII.17–VII.20b; the single-fixed-point statement; and the Jacobian $A$ as far as row 3, where the source's own conversion from PDF cuts off mid-entry. Its embedded figure (`11-outline/figures/p005-1.png`, page 5) is the professor's own redrawing of the stability diagram, with the regions and the conditions $a_3,a_4,c_1$ labelled directly — that image is the primary source for the stability-diagram figure and its labels in this chapter. - `lectures/11-notes.md` — the Atkinson et al. paper itself. Its embedded page images (`11-notes/figures/p002-1.jpeg`, the paper's Fig. 1A–F; `p003-1.png`, Fig. 2A–B gene architecture; `p004-1.jpeg`, Fig. 3A plasmid map and 3B–E data/model time courses) are the source for the circuit topology, the $\oplus/\ominus$ signs used to fix the sign of $g_{12},g_{14},g_{32}$, the two promoter variants, and the experimental validation mentioned at the end. The markdown text of this file is almost entirely figure-axis labels rather than body prose; no figure legend text was available, so the pairing of each promoter variant with switch versus oscillator behaviour is deliberately not stated here. - **Completed, not sourced**: the fourth row of $A$, the factorized determinant, the quartic coefficients $a_1,a_4$, and the general Routh–Hurwitz criterion for a quartic are worked out in this chapter directly from the equations above — the outline's transcription stops before this point. The explicit form of $a_2$, $a_3$ in full and of $c_1$ is not derived here. - **Referred to but not supplied**: the paper's Supplementary Information, which the outline itself cites for the derivation of the stability diagram's boundaries, and the figure legends for `11-notes.md`'s Figs. 1–3, which were not part of the extracted text.
